Summary judgment
- The evidence supports a real, specific difference: Model B (B − A) pushes the residual stream toward vocabulary about professional/academic topics and culinary/restaurant cooking vocabulary. In other words, B is relatively more likely than A to produce tokens like "professional/Professional", "dissertation", "doctoral", "undergraduate", "technical", "molecular", and a large cluster of culinary/restaurant words ("cooking", "Cooking", "restaurant", "Restaurant", "Chef", "kitchen", "baking", "Cake", "oven", "microwave", "Cook", etc.).

Why I conclude this
- Token-level readouts (logit lens) for the highest‑norm cells overwhelmingly list the same families of tokens across many middle-to-late layers: two clear semantic clusters appear — (1) professional/academic/technical terms (dissertation, doctoral, undergraduate, professional, technical, molecular, etc.) and (2) culinary/restaurant terms (cooking, Cooking, restaurant, Restaurant, Chef, kitchen, baking, oven, Cake, Cook, Baked, etc.). These tokens recur across many layers and positions (especially layers ≈16–25).
- The L2-norm map shows the difference is concentrated in middle-to-late layers and strongly at token position 1 (pos1 has especially large values in many layers, e.g. layers 15–25). That indicates the difference is applied early in the sequence and amplified through later layers, consistent with a change that biases the model toward particular topical vocabularies for subsequent decoding.
- The combination (consistent token directions + concentrated, high-magnitude activations at early positions in later layers) is evidence of a stable semantic shift rather than random noise.

Caveats / alternative hypotheses
- The two semantic clusters (academic/professional vs culinary) could reflect a single underlying style/objective (e.g., more "professional / commercial / service-oriented" language) or two separate tendencies introduced together; the evidence supports the lexical shift but does not uniquely identify the fine-tuning source. Possible causes include fine-tuning on restaurant/review/cookbook text, on professional bios/resumes, or on a corpus mixing both (e.g., local business directories, service listings).
- Patchscope continuations were not provided here, so I could not verify how the difference vector changes full-sentence continuations; my conclusion rests on the logit-lens token directions and the activation norms.

If you want, I can:
- Examine patchscope continuations (if you provide them) to see how the change affects generated text in context.
- Run a targeted probe (e.g., apply the difference vector to prompts about different domains) to disambiguate whether the shift is primarily culinary vs academic/professional vs a single stylistic change.
